paragraphs.text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome-4 (CDLS4) is a cohesinopathy caused by alterations in RAD21, a structural protein of the cohesin complex. It causes growth retardation, minor skeletal anomalies, and facial features that overlap those of classic Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS). Compared with CdLS caused by NIPBL or SMC1A variants, the phenotype is milder: facial morphology, limb anomalies, cognition and behavior are less severely affected (Deardorff et al., 2012; Krab et al., 2020). Some individuals with monoallelic RAD21 variants have holoprosencephaly, with or without CdLS features (Kruszka et al., 2019; Krab et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Krab et al. (2020) reported 49 individuals from 33 families with RAD21 alterations, including 24 previously unpublished cases. The patients came from Australia, Europe, Turkey, Canada and the United States. Full clinical information was available for 29 individuals from 22 families (cohort A), all of whom had CdLS clinical scores of at least 5. Their phenotype was an attenuated form of CdLS compared with that caused by NIPBL or SMC1A variants, with milder facial morphology, limb anomalies, cognition and behavior. The frequent features in cohort A were short nose (23/26), long and/or smooth philtrum (26/29), concave nasal ridge (24/29), thick eyebrows (20/24), long eyelashes (21/26), synophrys (19/28), thin upper lip vermilion (23/29), short fifth finger (23/28), postnatal microcephaly (16/28), and gastroesophageal reflux (13/25). No patient had major limb malformations (0/29) or visual impairment (0/24). Small hands (5/27), small feet (3/27), hirsutism (10/26) and seizures (2/22) were less common than in the NIPBL and SMC1A cohorts. Hearing loss was present in 8/24, heart defects in 9/23, and cleft palate in 6/25. Pregnancies and births were usually normal and prenatal growth retardation was uncommon. Short stature and microcephaly developed after birth. About half of the patients had congenital anomalies such as cleft palate and cardiac anomalies. Unusual findings included vertebral anomalies (clefts and hemivertebrae) and malformations of structures derived from the embryonic foregut. Diaphragmatic hernia, anal atresia or choanal atresia occurred occasionally. Cognition and behavior were also attenuated. Sixteen of 29 patients (55%) had normal or mildly impaired cognition, none had severe or profound disability, and all patients aged 3 years and older used some words. Problems were mainly language-based. Behavioral problems were present in 14 of 25 (56%), mainly anxiety, ADHD, autistic features and obsessive-compulsive behavior. Self-injurious behavior (1/18) and aggression (1/16) were infrequent.

paragraphs.text: Lei et al. (2020) described a 6-year-old Han Chinese boy, the first child of healthy unrelated parents, who had a de novo t(8; 18)(q22; q21) translocation. He had growth retardation (height and weight -2.0 SD), mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, and left-sided cleft palate. His congenital heart defect comprised a ventricular septal defect, double-outlet right ventricle, and juxtaposition of the aorta and pulmonary artery. He also had thoracic scoliosis, butterfly vertebrae, fifth-finger clinodactyly, fingerpads, umbilical and inguinal hernias, and recurrent respiratory infections. His facial dysmorphism included arched thick eyebrows, long eyelashes, a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nostrils, large prominent ears, dental malocclusion, and micrognathia. Kabuki syndrome was initially suspected. Multiple exostoses were found at age 10 years.

paragraphs.text: CDLS4 shows autosomal dominant inheritance. Minor et al. (2014) reported the first familial case: an intragenic RAD21 deletion inherited from the patient's mother. Boyle et al. (2017) found a RAD21 deletion in an index patient, her mother and 2 aunts, and suggested incomplete penetrance. Krab et al. (2020) noted that RAD21 variants were often familial (5 of 12 cohort A cases with known inheritance). Mildly affected parents were sometimes diagnosed only after their more severely affected offspring were recognized, so the authors recommended parental testing even when parents appear unaffected.

paragraphs.text: Pereza et al. (2015) revised their earlier diagnosis of Langer-Giedion syndrome in a girl with a 7.5-Mb interstitial deletion at 8q23.3q24.13. The deletion included EXT1 but not TRPS1. Because it also included RAD21 and 30 other RefSeq genes, the authors suggested that the correct diagnosis was CDLS4.
